rationale: Bird and Diz is the last studio meeting of bebop's two founders, cut on June 6, 1950 and issued in 1952 as a ten-inch LP with two Parker-only 1949 sides added [S1,S3] (obs). Session gravity is exceptional: the June 6 quintet is Parker and Gillespie with Thelonious Monk, Curley Russell and Buddy Rich [S1,S3,S4] (obs) — one of the very few occasions Parker recorded with Monk, and the final Parker-Gillespie studio date of their careers, the later reunion being the live Massey Hall concert [S1,S2] (obs). Consensus across independent listing traditions: AllMusic rates it four and a half stars and Rick Anderson's review calls it 'an outstanding album' with 'top-of-the-line production quality' [S1,S2] (obs); DownBeat's 1952 review gave four stars and the Penguide Guide to Jazz Recordings, The Encyclopedia of Popular Music and The Rolling Stone Jazz & Blues Album Guide all carry it with positive ratings [S1] (obs). Lineage: 'Bloomdido', 'Mohawk', 'Leap Frog' and 'Relaxin' with Lee' entered the bebop book and are played by every generation since, and the album stands with the founding bebop records the canon admitted on 2026-09-24, alongside The Charlie Parker Story and Bird on 52nd Street, both already held [S1,S2] (inf). It still plays: twenty-five minutes of the two men at full tilt, with 'Bloomdido' a career-best Parker blues head [S2] (obs). Against: it is a short ten-inch collection rather than a conceived LP statement; Monk is buried in the mix and gets almost no solo space [S2] (obs); and the version most listeners meet is a longer Verve reissue that mixes in takes and sessions beyond the original record [S1,S2] (obs). Priority strong rather than must_have for those reasons.

personnel_record.notes:
Three sessions across two years. June 6, 1950, New York City: Parker, Gillespie, Monk, Curley Russell, Buddy Rich — six tracks (Bloomdido, My Melancholy Baby, Relaxin' with Lee, Leap Frog, An Oscar for Treadwell, Mohawk). May 5, 1949, New York City: Parker, Dorham, Al Haig, Tommy Potter, Max Roach — 'Passport'. February-March 1949, New York City: Parker, Dorham, Tommy Turk, Al Haig, Tommy Potter, Max Roach and Carlos Vidal (bongos) — 'Visa'. The two 1949 sides were Parker-only dates on the original ten-inch LP; later Verve reissues omit them and substitute other Parker takes, so the LP's eight-track shape is recorded here, with the reissue takes excluded as alternate/bonus material.

Conflicts preserved: (1) Release year — Wikipedia gives July/August 1952 while AllMusic's release-date field says July 1, 1950 (its own review text says 1956); the album was recorded in 1950 and released in 1952, and 1950 is staged as the year, matching how the canon already dates archival bebop material (The Charlie Parker Story 1945, Groovin' High 1945, Birth of the Cool 1950). (2) 1949 date — Wikipedia's prose says the two extra tracks were cut 'in March and May 1949' but its own track table dates 'Visa' to 2/3/49 and 'Passport' to 5/5/49, while jazzdisco gives the septet session as 'February-March, 1949' and the quintet as 'May 5, 1949'. The table and jazzdisco are followed for 'Visa' (1949-02-03); the underlying ambiguity is noted. (3) Studio — Discogs states the June 6, 1950 session took place 'in an unknown recording studio, New York City'; jazzdisco gives only 'NYC'. No source consulted names a studio, so the NYC 'venue unidentified' place is used and no new place is minted. (4) Label — Wikipedia's infobox says Clef/Verve and its text says the 1952 issue came 'on the Verve subsidiary label Clef Records', while jazzdisco and Discogs show Mercury MGC-512 in 1952 and Clef MG C-512 in 1954; Clef is recorded as the label with the Mercury distribution noted. (5) Engineer — no source consulted credits an engineer for these sessions, so engineer is null. AllMusic also fills the style field with Big Band and Chamber Music alongside Bop; only Bop is staged as the primary style. Personnel for the two 1949 sessions is not separated per date by any source consulted, so both 1949 dates carry the same band except Turk and Vidal on 'Visa'.

ballot.album: Charlie Parker & Dizzy Gillespie — Bird and Diz (1950)
ballot.case_for: The June 1950 session brings together Parker, Gillespie, Monk, Curley Russell, and Buddy Rich for the final Parker–Gillespie studio date, giving it exceptional session gravity (S1, S3, S4). Its repertoire includes “Bloomdido,” “Mohawk,” “Leap Frog,” and “Relaxin’ with Lee,” while positive ratings across AllMusic, DownBeat, Penguin, Rolling Stone, and the Encyclopedia of Popular Music support its standing as a recognized bebop classic (S1, S2).
ballot.case_against: The original ten-inch LP is an awkwardly assembled object: six tracks come from the 1950 quintet session, while two Parker-only sides from 1949 were added, and later reissues often alter or expand that program (S1, S3, S5). Monk is reportedly buried in the mix and given little solo space (S2), and the session’s historical personnel distinction does not by itself make this a definitive Parker or Gillespie statement; the favorable guide ratings are solid but not uniformly top-tier.
ballot.disagreement: Both references support strong priority and agree the album is in scope, but they differ on tier: Reference 1 judges the positive consensus and session significance sufficient for consensus_core, while Reference 2 considers the compilation-like album construction and compromised session balance grounds for contested.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes John retain Bird and Diz as a strong, contested bebop candidate, weighing its exceptional session and repertoire against the limitations of the album as originally packaged.
